items: Science is a way of thinking, observing and doing things to understand the world — it starts from curiosity, it is everywhere, and like an unending jigsaw puzzle it keeps growing and changing.
Science = thinking + observing + doing, to understand the world.
Curiosity is the most important thing — that is why the book is called 'Curiosity'.
Science is everywhere — even in the kitchen and on the playground.
Science never ends and can change: new discoveries add pieces and sometimes move old ones.

notes.h: What Will We Explore in Science?
items: The book's science journey starts at home on planet Earth — living things, food, water, hot and cold, materials — and then goes beyond Earth to the Sun, the Moon and the stars; as we learn more we find these ideas are connected.
On Earth: life, food, water, hot and cold, materials.
Beyond Earth: the Sun, the Moon, the stars.
The more we discover, the more we see that these ideas are connected.

The scientific method is a step-by-step process to find answers: observe, ask a question, guess a possible answer, test the guess, and analyse the results — if the guess is wrong, make a new guess and test again.
Five steps in order: Observe → Question → Guess → Test → Analyse.
A guess is only a possible answer until it is tested.
A wrong guess is not a failure — make a new guess and test again.
Science is not just memorising facts or doing experiments — it is a step-by-step process.

Scientists follow the scientific method — and anyone who does so is working like a scientist. To think like one, be curious, observe keenly, ask how and why, work with others and keep exploring with joy.
Be curious — the first and foremost thing in learning science.
Observe your surroundings keenly.
Ask how and why — to be a wise person, be a 'whys' person.
Science is rarely done alone — scientists work in large teams; ask your friends.
Wrong: Science is only memorising facts and figures. Right: Science is a way of thinking, observing and doing — asking questions and finding out how things work
Wrong: Science is only about things on Earth. Right: The book also asks about things beyond Earth — the Sun, the Moon and the stars
Wrong: If the first guess is wrong, the scientific method has failed. Right: We make another guess and test it — the pen ink may have dried up instead of finishing
Wrong: Only people in laboratories are scientists. Right: Anyone who follows the scientific method — a cook, a cycle repairer, an electrician, you — works like a scientist

sol_items: What is science?: A way of thinking, observing and doing things to understand the world around us.
What will we explore with this book?: Living things, food, water, hot and cold, materials, magnets, light, motion and Earth and the sky.
How can we find answers to our questions on our ow: By following the scientific method.
Your pen stops writing. What would you do?: Check the ink, shake it, try on another paper and test a refill; this is a step-by-step search for the cause.
What steps can we follow to find answers?: Observe, ask a question, guess an answer, test the guess and analyse the result.

notes.h: Diversity in Plants and Animals Around Us
items: Plants and animals around us show great variety in their features; this variety in a region is its biodiversity, and every member has a role, so plants and animals depend on each other.
Observe without disturbing; do not pluck leaves and flowers
Variety of plants and animals in a region = its biodiversity
Each member has a role; plants and animals depend on each other
Plants and animals can be grouped on the basis of their common features; different groups may choose different bases, and grouping makes them easier to understand and study.
Basis = the common feature used to make groups
Different students may choose different bases
Grouping makes plants and animals easier to understand and study

By height, kind of stem and where branches start, plants are grouped into herbs, shrubs and trees; plants with weak stems that need support are climbers, and plants that creep along the ground are creepers.
Tree: tall, thick woody trunk, branches high
Shrub: bushy, hard stems branching near the ground
Herb: small, soft green stem
Climbers: weak stems, need support · Creepers: creep along the ground
The thin lines on a leaf are veins; their pattern is venation — a net-like pattern is reticulate venation and veins running side by side is parallel venation.
Venation = pattern of veins
Reticulate = net (hibiscus)
Parallel = side by side (banana, grass)

A taproot system has one main root with small side roots; a fibrous root system is a bunch of similar thin roots from the base of the stem. Generally reticulate venation goes with taproots and parallel venation with fibrous roots.
Taproot = one main root + side roots
Fibrous = bunch of thin roots from stem base
Reticulate ↔ taproot; parallel ↔ fibrous (generally)

Each part of a seed is a cotyledon; plants whose seeds have two cotyledons are dicots and one cotyledon are monocots. Dicots have reticulate venation and taproots; monocots have parallel venation and fibrous roots.
Cotyledon = part of the seed
Dicot: 2 cotyledons, reticulate, taproot
Monocot: 1 cotyledon, parallel, fibrous

Animals move in different ways — fly, walk, run, crawl, hop or jump, swim — using different body parts such as wings, legs and fins; movement, and other features like food, home, shape, size and colour, can be used to group animals.
Movement: fly, walk, run, crawl, hop/jump, swim
Body parts: wings, legs, fins
Other bases: food, home, colour, shape, size, structure
Biodiversity varies from region to region because conditions differ; special features that enable plants and animals to survive in a particular region are adaptations.
Biodiversity varies because conditions vary
Adaptation = special feature to survive in a region
Desert: store water/food, save water · Mountains: shed snow, short legs, long hair · Water: streamlined body, fins

The place where plants and animals live is their habitat; it provides food, water, air and shelter. By habitat, living things are grouped as terrestrial (land) and aquatic (water); amphibians like frogs live in both.
Habitat gives food, water, air, shelter
Terrestrial = land; aquatic = water; frog = both
Habitat shapes the biodiversity of a region
When habitats are damaged, plants and animals lose their homes, food and other resources, and biodiversity is lost; governments, communities and scientists work to protect it.
Habitat damage → loss of homes, food, resources → loss of biodiversity
Projects: Project Tiger 1973, Cheetah Reintroduction 2022, Bustard protected areas
Sacred groves, Silent Valley — people protect biodiversity
Wrong: Biodiversity means only wild animals like tigers and elephants. Right: It is the variety of ALL plants and animals of a region — grass, ants and crows too
Wrong: There is only one right way to group living things. Right: Any common feature can be a basis; different bases give different groups, all correct
Wrong: Any plant that is not tall is a herb. Right: Check the stem: a rose plant is only medium in height but has hard woody stems — a shrub
Wrong: All leaves have the same pattern of veins. Right: Some have a net (reticulate — hibiscus); some have veins running side by side (parallel — banana, grass)
Wrong: A thick root that we eat, like radish, is not a real root kind. Right: Radish is a swollen main root — a taproot
Wrong: A dicot is a plant with two seeds. Right: Di = two cotyledons inside ONE seed

sol_items: Why do we group books and notebooks? Importance of: Grouping makes things easy to find and to study.
Differences among herbs, shrubs and trees: Herbs are small with soft green stems; shrubs are bushy with branches near the base; trees are tall with a thick trunk.
Do veins make groups? Net-like and parallel venati: Yes: leaves with net-like veins are reticulate; with lines side by side are parallel.
Relation between venation and kind of root: Plants with reticulate venation have taproots; plants with parallel venation have fibrous roots.
Are all seeds similar? Dicots and monocots: No. Dicot seeds split into two halves (two cotyledons); monocot seeds have one.
Wheat and kidney bean: Wheat: fibrous roots, parallel venation. Kidney bean: taproot, reticulate venation.
imp_items: Why do we group plants?
It makes study easy
Differentiate a herb and a tree.
A herb is small and soft stemmed; a tree is tall with a trunk
What is leaf venation?
The pattern of veins in a leaf
Name two kinds of root systems.
Taproot and fibrous root
Differentiate dicots and monocots.
Dicots have two cotyledons; monocots have one
Which root goes with parallel venation?
Fibrous root

items: People across India eat many kinds of food. The traditional food of a state is usually based on the crops grown there, which depend on soil and climate; taste, culture and traditions also shape food choices.
India is an agricultural country with diverse soil and climate, so different crops grow in different regions
Traditional food is usually based on locally grown crops
Food choice also depends on taste preferences, culture and traditions
Cooking (culinary) practices have changed over time: chulha → modern gas stove, sil-batta → electrical grinder, because of technological development, improved transport and better communication.
Traditional and modern culinary practices differ a lot
Reasons for change: technological development, improved transportation, better communication
Food gives energy. Carbohydrates are one of the primary sources of energy in our diet; glucose gives instant energy; common sugar and starch are carbohydrates.
Carbohydrates = main energy source
Glucose → instant energy
Sugar and starch are carbohydrates
Ghee, oils, butter, nuts and seeds are rich in fat, which comes from plants and animals. Fat is a source of stored energy. Carbohydrates and fats together are called energy-giving foods.
Fat = stored energy
From plants (nuts, seeds, oils) and animals (butter, ghee, curd)
Carbohydrates + fats = energy-giving foods
Protein-rich foods help in growth and repair of the body, so they are called body-building foods. They come from plants (pulses, beans, peas, nuts) and animals (milk, paneer, egg, fish, meat).
Proteins = growth and repair = body-building
Plant and animal sources
Children and sportspersons need enough protein

Vitamins A, B1, C and D are needed in small amounts but protect the body from diseases. Lack of a vitamin for a long time causes a deficiency disease. Some vitamins are lost in cooking and washing cut vegetables; vitamin D is made by our body in sunlight.
Vitamins: small amount, big protection
A eyes · B1 heart · C fight disease · D bones (with calcium)
Eat some fruits and uncooked vegetables

Minerals — calcium, iodine and iron — are needed in small amounts and protect the body; lack causes bone and tooth decay, goitre and anaemia. Iodised salt is common salt mixed with salts of iodine. Vitamins and minerals together are called protective nutrients.
Calcium → bones and teeth · Iodine → goitre if lacking · Iron → blood (anaemia)
Iodised salt = salt + iodine salts
Vitamins + minerals = protective nutrients

Besides the five nutrients, the body needs dietary fibres (roughage) and water. Roughage gives no nutrients but helps remove undigested food and ensures smooth passage of stools; it comes mainly from plant products. Water helps absorb nutrients and removes waste through sweat and urine.
Roughage gives no nutrients; roughage and water are needed besides the five nutrients
Roughage → smooth stools; mainly from plants
Water → absorb nutrients, remove waste
Starch, a kind of carbohydrate, is detected by putting 2–3 drops of dilute iodine solution on a food: a blue-black colour shows starch is present.
Iodine + starch → blue-black
All starches are carbohydrates; not all carbohydrates are starches
A blue-black result on potato shows a liquid is likely iodine solution
Fat is detected by pressing a food inside paper: an oily patch through which light faintly shines shows that the food contains fat.
Oily patch + light shines through = fat
Let wet items dry first — a water patch disappears

Protein is detected by mixing a food paste with water, 2 drops of copper sulfate solution and 10 drops of caustic soda solution: a violet colour shows protein. Table 3.3 shows that one food may contain several nutrients.
Copper sulfate + caustic soda → violet = protein
One food may have more than one nutrient (peanuts)
Handle chemicals with care

A diet that has all essential nutrients, roughage and water in the right amount for proper growth and development is a balanced diet. The kind and amount of nutrients needed vary with age, gender, physical activity, health status and lifestyle.
Balanced = all nutrients + roughage + water, right amount
Needs vary: age, gender, activity, health, lifestyle

Junk foods have high calories from much sugar and fat but very little protein, minerals, vitamins and fibre (potato wafers, candy bars, carbonated drinks); eating them often makes a person obese and unhealthy. Nutrition labels help us choose; fortified foods have nutrients added.
Junk = high sugar/fat, low protein, vitamins, minerals, fibre
Frequent junk food → obesity and health problems
Packaged food must list its nutrients
'Health is the Ultimate Wealth'

Millets — jowar, bajra, ragi and sanwa — are small-sized grains native to India that grow easily in different climates. They are rich in vitamins, minerals (iron, calcium) and dietary fibre, so they are called nutri-cereals and contribute to a balanced diet.
Millets: jowar, bajra, ragi, sanwa
Grow easily in different climates
Part of the Indian diet for centuries; popular again for health benefits
Help a balanced diet — but cannot be the whole diet

Food travels from farm to plate through many steps and people. The whole distance a food item travels from producer to consumer is its food miles; reducing food miles cuts cost and pollution, supports local farmers and keeps food fresh. We must not waste food.
Food miles = producer → consumer distance
Fewer food miles: cheaper, cleaner, fresher, supports farmers
Do not waste food
Wrong: People all over India eat the same kind of food. Right: Food varies from state to state; some items are common, many are special to one state
Wrong: Cooking practices have stayed the same for hundreds of years. Right: They have changed a lot — chulha to gas stove, sil-batta to electrical grinder
Wrong: Only sweet foods are carbohydrates. Right: Rice, wheat and potato are not sweet but are rich in carbohydrate (starch)
Wrong: Fat comes only from animals. Right: Many plant foods — nuts, seeds, oils, coconut — are rich in fat
Wrong: Only meat and eggs give protein. Right: Pulses, beans, peas, nuts, soya bean, milk, paneer and mushrooms also give protein
Wrong: Vitamins are needed in large amounts like rice or dal. Right: They are needed in small amounts but are essential

sol_items: Why is traditional food different across states?: It depends on the crops, climate and customs of each region.
Have food habits and cooking changed over time? Wh: Yes. Chulha gave way to gas, and sil-batta to mixers, because of new technology and busy life.
Why does a marathon runner drink glucose water?: Glucose gives quick energy.
Why do we prefer laddoos in winter?: They contain fat and carbohydrate for energy and warmth.
Why include fruits and vegetables in our diet?: They give vitamins, minerals and fibre.
Case 1 (scurvy) and Case 2 (iodised salt): Scurvy is cured by vitamin C (lemon, amla). Iodised salt contains added iodine to prevent goitre.

items: A magnet attracts iron things. Some magnets occur in nature (lodestones); most we use are artificial and are made in many shapes.
Natural magnet = lodestone
Artificial magnets are made from iron and other materials
Shapes: bar, U-shaped, ring (also disc, cylindrical, spherical)
A magnet attracts only some materials. Materials attracted by a magnet are magnetic (iron, nickel, cobalt); the rest are non-magnetic.
Magnetic = attracted (iron, nickel, cobalt)
Non-magnetic = not attracted (wood, plastic, rubber, glass)
The attraction of a magnet is strongest near its two ends — the North pole and the South pole. Poles always come in pairs.
Two poles: North and South
Strongest attraction at the poles
Poles always in pairs — no single pole

notes.h: A Freely Suspended Magnet Rests North–South
items: A magnet that can turn freely always comes to rest along the north–south direction, because the Earth behaves like a giant magnet. An iron bar does not — so this is a test for a magnet.
Freely suspended magnet rests N–S
End pointing north = North (north-seeking) pole
Earth behaves like a giant magnet
Iron bar rests in any direction → test for a magnet

A magnetic compass has a freely turning needle-shaped magnet that rests north–south; turning the dial to line up with it gives all directions. We can make one with a magnetised needle on a floating cork.
Compass needle = small magnet that rotates freely
Red end usually points north
Line up the dial with the needle
Stroke a needle 30–40 times with one pole → it becomes a magnet
Unlike poles (N–S) of two magnets attract; like poles (N–N, S–S) repel. Only a magnet can repel a magnet, so repulsion is the sure test of a magnet.
Unlike poles attract
Like poles repel
Repulsion = sure test of a magnet
A magnet's effect passes through non-magnetic materials like wood, cardboard, plastic and glass — the compass needle deflects the same with or without them.
Magnetic effect passes through wood, cardboard, plastic, glass
A magnet can move things without touching them
Toys and tricks with magnets use their properties: attracting iron, acting through non-magnetic materials, and like poles repelling. Magnets must be stored in pairs and handled with care.
Garland → attraction of iron
Maze, clip in water → acts through non-magnetic materials
Cars, frog → like poles repel
Store in pairs: unlike poles same side, wood between, soft iron across ends
Wrong: All magnets are natural stones dug out of the ground. Right: Lodestones are natural, but magnets in labs, pencil boxes and toys are artificial — made by people
Wrong: A magnet attracts every metal. Right: Only some metals — iron, nickel, cobalt (and some of their combinations) are magnetic; aluminium and copper are not (added)
Wrong: The middle of a magnet is the strongest part. Right: Attraction is strongest at the poles, near the ends; the middle holds very few filings
Wrong: Any iron bar hung by a thread points north–south. Right: Only a magnet does; an iron bar can rest in any direction
Wrong: A compass needle shows only north. Right: It shows the north–south line; after lining up the dial we can read every direction
Wrong: If something is attracted by a magnet, it must be a magnet. Right: Iron is also attracted (at both ends); only repulsion proves it is a magnet

sol_items: Do magnets attract all materials? Which materials : No. Only iron, steel, nickel and cobalt things are magnetic; wood, plastic, glass and paper are non-magnetic.
Do iron filings stick all over a magnet?: No; they stick mostly near the two ends, the poles.
Can a magnet have a single pole?: No. Every magnet has two poles, even a broken piece.
Suspended magnet at rest: It always rests along the north-south direction.
Does a suspended iron bar rest north-south?: No, an iron bar is not a magnet.
How can we make a compass?: Magnetise a needle, float it on a leaf in water, and it points north-south.

Iron and nickel

Wood and plastic
Where is a magnet strongest?
At the two ends, the poles
What are the names of the two poles?
North pole and south pole
How do like and unlike poles behave?
Like poles repel; unlike poles attract
Can we get a magnet with one pole?
No, every magnet has two poles

items: To measure a length we compare it with a unit; the result is a number and a unit. Body-part units like the handspan differ from person to person, so the same length gets different numbers.
Measuring = comparing with a unit
Length = number + unit
Body-part units differ from person to person — we need a unit that does not

Countries adopted the International System of Units (SI). The SI unit of length is the metre (m); kilometre is used for large lengths and centimetre, millimetre for small ones: 1 km = 1000 m, 1 m = 100 cm, 1 cm = 10 mm.
SI unit of length = metre (m)
km for long distances, cm and mm for small lengths

Scale in contact along the length
Eye directly above

items: A curved length is measured with a flexible measuring tape, or with a thread laid along the curve, straightened and measured on a metre scale.
Flexible tape or thread for curves
Straighten the thread, then use the metre scale
Thread must not stretch
A distance means something only when we say 'from where'. The fixed object or point from which distance is stated is the reference point; the distance from it gives the position.
Always ask: distance from what?
Reference point = fixed object/point
Position = distance from the reference point

An object is in motion if its position changes with respect to the reference point with time; it is at rest if its position does not change. The same object can be at rest for one reference point and in motion for another.
Motion: position changes with time w.r.t. reference point
Rest: position does not change
Change the reference point → the answer may change
When an object moves along a straight line, its motion is called linear motion.
Linear = straight-line path
When an object moves along a circular path, its motion is called circular motion.
Circular = circular path, round and round

When an object moves to and fro about some fixed position, its motion is called oscillatory motion. If an object repeats its path after a fixed interval of time its motion is periodic — circular and oscillatory motions are periodic.
Oscillatory = to and fro about a fixed position
Periodic = repeats after a fixed time
Circular and oscillatory are periodic
Real motions are sorted by their path; a long path may have parts of different kinds.
Wrong: If two people get different numbers for the same table, one of them measured wrongly. Right: Both can be careful — their handspans (units) are of different sizes
Wrong: 1 km = 100 m (or 1 km = 100 cm). Right: 1 km = 1000 m = 1,00,000 cm
Wrong: If the zero mark is broken, the scale cannot be used. Right: Start from any full mark (say 1.0 cm) and subtract it from the other reading
Wrong: A curve cannot be measured with a straight metre scale at all. Right: Lay a thread along it, straighten the thread and then measure the thread on the scale

Wrong: An object is either moving or at rest — it does not depend on anything. Right: It depends on the reference point: passengers are at rest w.r.t. the bus, in motion w.r.t. a building

sol_items: Why does the number of handspans differ for each f: Hands differ in size, so body-part units are not the same for all. A standard unit gives the same result.

Soft = compressed or scratched easily

notes.h: Choosing a Material for an Object
items: We choose a material for an object depending on its properties and the purpose for which the object is to be used.
Purpose → needed properties → material
Different parts of one object can be of different materials
Wrong: 'Material' means only cloth (dress material). Right: Any substance used to make an object — wood, metal, plastic, clay, paper — is a material
Wrong: There is only one correct way to group a set of objects. Right: The groups depend on the property chosen — shape, colour, material … all are correct if each group shares that property
Wrong: Everything that shines is a metal. Right: Polished or wax/plastic-coated surfaces shine too, but they may not be metals
Wrong: Every material is simply 'hard' or 'soft' for ever. Right: Hardness is relative — rubber is hard compared with sponge and soft compared with iron

Why are different materials used for different bal: Each game needs a ball with its own bounce, hardness and weight.

items: Our sense of touch can mislead us, so we use temperature — measured with a thermometer — as the reliable measure of how hot or cold a body is.
Touch is not reliable
Temperature = reliable measure of hotness or coldness
Hotter body → higher temperature
Thermometer measures temperature
A clinical thermometer measures human body temperature; normal is taken as 37.0 °C, the average of many healthy people, and the body stays between 35 °C and 42 °C.
Clinical = body temperature
Digital replaces mercury (toxic)
Normal 37.0 °C (an average)
Body stays 35–42 °C

items: The same temperature can be written on three scales: Celsius (°C), Fahrenheit (°F) and Kelvin (K); kelvin is the SI unit and K = °C + 273.15.
Celsius, Fahrenheit and Kelvin are named after the scientists who developed them
SI unit = kelvin

notes.h: Laboratory Thermometer: Range and Smallest Value
items: A laboratory thermometer is a sealed glass tube with a liquid-filled bulb and a Celsius scale; before using it we find its range and the smallest value one division reads.
Range: usually −10 °C to 110 °C
Smallest value = difference ÷ divisions
Reading = last numbered mark + divisions × smallest value

items: A laboratory thermometer gives a correct reading only when its bulb is fully in the liquid without touching the container, it is held vertical, it is read while still in the liquid, and the eye is level with the top of the column.
Bulb free in the liquid
Vertical
Read while immersed
Eye at level of column top

Room thermometer → approximate room temperature
Weather reports → maximum and minimum
Changes daily and with seasons
Anna Mani — Weather Woman of India
Wrong: Touching is enough to know exactly how hot something is. Right: Touch compares with what the hand felt just before; the same water can feel cool to one hand and warm to the other

Wrong: Count the tick LINES between two numbers to get the divisions. Right: Count the SPACES — 11 lines make 10 divisions

sol_items: Can we judge fever by touch?: No. Touch can mislead.

items: Ice, water and water vapour are the same substance in three states — solid, liquid and gas. Ice keeps its shape; water flows and takes the shape of its container with the same volume; water vapour spreads into all the space.
Water has three states: solid (ice), liquid (water), gas (water vapour)
Solid — fixed shape; liquid — shape of container, fixed volume; gas — spreads into all the space
Other substances (wax, oil, ghee) also have states

Melting: solid → liquid on heating
Freezing: liquid → solid on cooling
Melting and freezing are opposite changes of the same substance
Water disappears from puddles, plates and pans because it changes into invisible water vapour — evaporation. Evaporation goes on all the time, even at room temperature.
Evaporation: water → water vapour
It goes on all the time, even at room temperature
Vapour is invisible; it mixes with the air

Faster: more exposed area, more heat, more air movement

Test one condition at a time
Evaporation needs heat; water evaporating from a surface takes that heat from the surface and the things near it, so they cool — the cooling effect. Matka, surahi and the pot-in-pot cooler use it.
Evaporation takes heat from the surface
So evaporation causes cooling
Matka, surahi, pot-in-pot cooler, sweat, sprinkling water

When water vapour in the air touches a cold surface it changes into water droplets — condensation. That is why droplets form outside a glass of ice water, dew forms on plants, and drops collect under the lid of a pot of boiling water.

Needs a cold surface
Scientists observe → ask questions → list possible reasons → test with experiments

notes.h: How Clouds Form and Give Rain
items: Air carrying water vapour rises; higher up it cools, and the vapour condenses around dust particles into tiny droplets that float as clouds. Droplets join into heavy drops that fall as rain — or, under special conditions, as hail or snow.
Vapour rises → cools → condenses on dust → clouds
Droplets join → heavy → rain, hail or snow
Clouds are condensation in the sky

Water from oceans and the Earth's surface evaporates, condenses into clouds and returns as rain, hail or snow, finally flowing back to the oceans — the water cycle. Only a small part of Earth's water is usable, so we must use it wisely.
Evaporation → condensation (clouds) → rain/hail/snow → back to the oceans
Most of Earth's water is in oceans and cannot be used directly
Rising population increases demand and causes water shortage — save water (more in 'Nature's Treasures')
Wrong: Ice and water are different substances because ice can be held and water cannot. Right: They are the same substance in two states; ice left in a cup becomes water

Wrong: Water in a matka is cold because clay itself is a cold material. Right: Water seeps through the clay and evaporates from the outside, taking heat from the water
Wrong: The water outside the tumbler seeped out through the glass. Right: The level inside does not go down and the mass increases — the water came from the air

sol_items: Are ice and water different substances?: No. They are the same substance, water, in different states.
Is something added to ice in the freezer?: No. Water only loses heat and freezes.
Where do puddles go? Where else do you see it?: Water slowly turns into vapour (evaporation) and mixes with the air; also wet clothes dry.
Water sprinkled on a hot dosa pan: It sizzles and quickly turns into vapour.
How does the smell of cooking reach us?: Gases spread in all directions and mix with the air.

notes.h: Mixtures and Why We Separate Them
items: A mixture has two or more substances mixed together. We separate them either to remove a part that is not useful or to get two different useful parts.
A mixture has two or more substances mixed.
Purpose 1: remove a part that is not useful.
Purpose 2: separate two parts that are both useful.
Picking out a component by hand, using differences in size, colour and shape — convenient when the part to remove is small in quantity and easy to pick.
Handpicking uses size, colour, shape.
Best when the part to remove is small in quantity.
Its purpose is sorting.
Threshing beats grains off the stalks; winnowing then uses wind to blow away the lighter husk while the heavier grains fall close by.
Threshing: beat stalks → loose grains.
Winnowing: wind → light husk away, heavy grains stay.
Threshers do both together.
A sieve lets small particles pass through its holes and keeps the bigger ones — used when the solids of a mixture differ in size.
Sieving uses particle size.
Small passes, big stays.
Choose holes between the two sizes.
A magnet pulls magnetic substances such as iron out of a mixture and leaves the non-magnetic ones behind.
Magnetic separation uses the magnetic property.
Iron is magnetic; sawdust is not.
Used in recycling.
Left undisturbed, the heavier insoluble part settles at the bottom (sedimentation); the liquid above is then poured off by tilting the vessel (decantation). It is quick but not complete.
Settle first, then pour.
Works for heavy insoluble solids and for oil and water.
Quick but not complete.
A filter has pores: insoluble particles bigger than the pores stay on it as residue and the clear liquid passes through as filtrate. Finer pores catch finer particles.
Filter pores decide what stays.
Residue on the filter; filtrate goes through.
More complete than decantation.
Churning curd makes the lighter butter collect and float on top, leaving buttermilk behind.
Churning: butter from curd.
Butter is lighter — floats.
Both parts are useful.
When a solution is left in sun and air or heated, the liquid turns into vapour and the dissolved solid is left behind; condensing the vapour gets the liquid back too.
Evaporation separates a dissolved solid from a liquid.
Sun and air or heating.
Condensation gets the liquid back.
Find the difference between the components to choose the method; a mixture of many components needs several methods in the right order.
Find the difference → choose the method.
Several components → several methods.
Order: big/magnetic first, dissolve → filter → evaporate last.
Wrong: We separate only to throw away the bad part. Right: Often both parts are useful — butter and buttermilk from curd
Wrong: Handpicking works for any mixture. Right: Only when the unwanted particles are big enough to see and pick, and few in number
Wrong: Winnowing separates grains from the stalks. Right: Threshing separates grains from stalks; winnowing separates husk from grains
Wrong: Any sieve works for any mixture. Right: The hole size must lie between the sizes of the two kinds of particles
Wrong: A magnet pulls out every metal. Right: Only magnetic substances such as iron; aluminium, copper and brass stay behind
Wrong: Sedimentation and decantation are the same step. Right: Sedimentation is the settling; decantation is the pouring that follows

sol_items: Puffed rice and chana dal: Sieving can work if the sizes differ, or use winnowing (puffed rice is light).
How do farmers separate grains from husk?: By threshing and then winnowing; wind blows the lighter husk away.
Husk in a closed room: Use a fan or blow gently, or open a window.
Do all sieve holes have the same size?: Holes in one sieve are the same size, but different sieves differ. Large holes let everything pass.

What is left on black paper when salt water dries?: White patches of salt are left; the water changed into vapour.

What is winnowing? Where is it used?

How is iron separated from sand?

notes.h: Movement, Growth and Response to Stimuli
items: Living beings move, grow and respond to stimuli. Plants do all three too, even though they do not move from place to place.
Compare anything with yourself to test if it is living
Plants show movement of parts, not of the whole plant
All living beings respond to stimuli
Living beings take food and air in and give wastes out: they need nutrition, they respire and they excrete — plants too.
Food in = nutrition; air in and out = respiration; wastes out = excretion
All living beings respire and excrete

notes.h: Reproduction, Death and Living vs Non-living
items: All living beings reproduce and eventually die. Something is living only if it shows all the characteristics; absence of any of them shows it is non-living.
Reproduction keeps life going
All features together = living; any one missing = non-living
Dead = once living, now cannot show the features

notes.h: Essential Conditions for Germination of a Seed
items: A seed germinates (turns into a sprout) when it gets the right amount of water and air. Most seeds do not need light to germinate, but the seedling needs sunlight to grow further.
Germination needs the right amount of water and air
Like our balanced diet ('Mindful Eating'), plants need nutrients and favourable conditions to grow
Whichever way a seedling is placed, its root grows downwards and its shoot grows upwards and towards sunlight.
Root → downwards
Shoot → upwards and towards light
A seed grows into a young plant, which matures to produce flowers and then fruits with seeds; the seeds give rise to the next generation. This whole journey is the life cycle of a plant.
Seed → germination → leaves → flowers → fruits with seeds → new plants
The plant dies after making seeds; its seeds continue the cycle
A mosquito passes through four very different-looking stages — egg, larva, pupa and adult. Eggs are laid on or near water; larvae and pupae live in water and come to the surface for air.
Egg → Larva → Pupa → Adult
Young stages live in water but need air
No stagnant water = no mosquito breeding
A frog passes through four stages — egg (spawn, then embryo), tadpole (with tail, then with legs), froglet and adult. Its body shape and even its home change: from water to water and land.
Egg → Tadpole → Froglet → Adult
Tail for swimming, strong legs for jumping
Habitat: water → water and land
Wrong: Anything that moves is living. Right: A car moves but never grows and never has young ones — movement alone does not prove life
Wrong: Breathing and respiration are exactly the same. Right: Breathing (air in and out) is only a part of respiration
Wrong: If a thing shows one or two features of life, it is living. Right: It must show all of them; absence of any one shows it is non-living — a car moves but is non-living
Wrong: Seeds need sunlight to germinate. Right: Bean seeds germinated in the dark pot C; most seeds do not need light to germinate — the seedling needs sunlight later
Wrong: A seedling turned upside down keeps growing upside down. Right: In beaker B the root bent to grow down and the shoot bent to grow up
Wrong: When the flower dries, that is the end of the flower. Right: The remaining parts of the flower develop into a fruit (pod) with seeds

sol_items: Why is a pencil non-living but a pigeon living?: The pigeon eats, grows, breathes, responds and reproduces; a pencil does none of these.
A car moves: is it living? What can you do that a car c...: No. A car cannot grow, eat, reproduce or respond like a living thing.
Do plants respire? Do plants move?: Yes. Plants respire and show slow movements such as bending to light and closing of touch-me-not leaves.
Three stimuli and responses: Bright light: close eyes; a pin prick: pull the hand; a loud noise: cover ears.
Young ones of five animals: Puppy, kitten, calf, chick and tadpole. Non-living things have no young ones.
Why is reproduction necessary?: It keeps the kind of living being going.
imp_items: Write four characteristics of living things.
Move, grow, respire and reproduce
What is a stimulus?
A change around us that makes us respond
Are plants living? Give two reasons.
Yes; they grow and respond to light
Differentiate living and non-living things.
Living things breathe, grow, reproduce; non-living do not
What do seeds need to germinate?
Water, air and suitable temperature
In which direction does a root grow?
Downwards, while the shoot grows upwards

topics: What Is a Natural Resource?
Natural resources are the treasures we get from nature — air, water, energy from the Sun, forests, soil, rocks, minerals, fossil ...

items: Natural resources are the treasures we get from nature — air, water, energy from the Sun, forests, soil, rocks, minerals, fossil fuels. We need them to survive and to make life comfortable; things people make from them are human-made resources.
Without nature's treasures no form of life on Earth is possible
We all are a part of nature
The chapter's treasures: air, water, energy from the Sun, forests, soil, rocks, minerals, fossil fuels

Air is a mixture of gases — mostly nitrogen, then oxygen — and we need its oxygen to survive. Moving air is wind, which turns firkis and windmills that can grind flour, pull water and make electricity.
We can live a few days without food or water, but not even a few minutes without oxygen
Most living beings need oxygen to survive
Air = a mixture of gases, not one gas

We need water for drinking, cooking, cleaning, crops and industry. Water covers about two-thirds of the Earth, but most of it is salty; only a very small part of the freshwater is easy to reach, and pollution makes even that unfit.
Water covers about two-thirds of the Earth's surface
Freshwater sources are limited — there is shortage in many parts of India; some people walk long distances for drinking water
Not everyone has the same access to water
Because freshwater is limited, we must reduce wastage, recycle water, prevent pollution and harvest rainwater — an age-old practice in India seen in stepwells.
Rainwater is harvested in many homes, societies and schools
Stepwells were built as a response to scarcity of water
World Water Day — 22 March every year

The Sun gives heat and light. Plants use sunlight to make food, animals eat plants and we eat both, so the Sun is the main source of energy on the Earth; solar devices capture its energy for electricity, cooking and heating water.
The Sun is the main source of energy on the Earth
Plants get energy from the Sun → animals eat plants → we get food from both
Without the Sun no life on Earth

Forests are large areas with dense growth of many kinds of plants. They give food, shelter and products, hold and enrich the soil, and support every life form — but they are shrinking and take many years to regrow, so we must protect them.
Forests are a natural home for wild animals, birds and insects
Every animal depends on other life forms; diversity ensures food for every living being

Soil holds sand, pebbles, roots, worms, insects, tiny organisms and decayed plants and animals; the air spaces in it help roots grow. It forms very slowly when rocks are broken apart by the Sun, water and living organisms, and different soils suit different uses.
Space between soil particles gives air and room for roots
Different colours = different materials in the soil
Soil supports biodiversity — a precious treasure

Rocks are used to build houses, roads and dams and once to make tools; they are made up of minerals, from which metals like iron, copper, aluminium and gold are extracted for cars, planes, jewellery and phones. Rocks take thousands to millions of years to form.
Rocks take thousands to millions of years to form — conserve them
Rocks and minerals are moved by vehicles that mostly run on fossil fuels

Petroleum, natural gas and coal are fossil fuels, formed over millions of years from buried remains of microorganisms and plants. They run vehicles, cook food and make electricity, but they are limited and burning them pollutes the air — so we must save them.

Renewable resources (air, water, forest) are renewed, replenished or restored by nature within a reasonable time; non-renewable ones (minerals, soil, rocks, coal, petroleum, natural gas) are limited and once used are exhausted.

Every daily activity uses natural resources directly or indirectly. We must conserve them and use them without waste — choosing cleaner alternatives — so that we meet today's needs and save for the future without harming the environment.
Conserve natural resources and use them responsibly
Meet present needs while saving for the future, without harming the environment
Wrong: Machines are a resource found in nature. Right: Machines are human-made resources — people make them from natural resources such as metals
Wrong: Air is mostly oxygen. Right: Air is mostly nitrogen (78%); oxygen is 21%
Wrong: Two-thirds of the Earth is water, so water can never run short. Right: Most of it is salty; only a very small fraction is freshwater that is easy to reach
Wrong: Rainwater harvesting is a new modern idea. Right: It is an age-old practice in India — stepwells like Bawadi and Vav
Wrong: An animal standing in sunlight gets its energy directly from the Sun. Right: Animals get energy from food; the food chain starts with plants that use sunlight
Wrong: If a forest is cut, planting saplings gives it back in a year or two. Right: It takes many years to grow a new forest or restore a lost one

sol_items: More treasures of nature: Soil, sunlight, forests, minerals and rocks.
Hold your breath: You feel uneasy because the body needs oxygen from air.
Name gases in the air: Nitrogen, oxygen, carbon dioxide and water vapour.
Where do we get water from?: Rain, rivers, lakes, ponds, wells and groundwater.
Human activities that pollute water; how to reduce: Dumping waste and washing; do not litter and use dustbins.
Ways to conserve water: Close taps, mend leaks, harvest rain and reuse water.
imp_items: What is a natural resource?
A treasure we get from nature
Name four natural resources.
Air, water, soil and forests
Differentiate renewable and non-renewable resources.
Renewable resources come back; non-renewable run out
Give two examples of each.
Renewable: air and water; non-renewable: coal and petrol
How can we use natural resources wisely? Give five points.
Save water, save fuel, plant trees, reduce waste and reuse things
Name two gases in air.
Nitrogen and oxygen

topics: Stars and Constellations
Stars shine with their own light
Pole Star and Finding Directions
The Pole Star (Dhruva tārā), in the Little Dipper, appears nearly stationary in the North, so it shows the North direction in the ...
Night Sky Watching
Stars are best seen from dark, open places on clear, moonless nights; light pollution, smoke, dust, clouds and buildings hide them
The Sun
The Sun is a star — the closest one — a hot ball of gases giving heat and light
Planets
A planet is a large, nearly spherical object that revolves around the Sun
Natural Satellites and the Moon
Objects that move around planets are satellites; moons are natural satellites
Asteroids and Comets
Asteroids are small, rocky, irregular objects, many revolving between Mars and Jupiter
Our Solar System — All Members Together
The Sun, eight planets, their moons and smaller objects such as asteroids and comets form the Solar System
The Milky Way Galaxy and the Universe

items: Stars shine with their own light. People joined groups of stars with imaginary lines into patterns — constellations — and today the sky is divided into 88 constellation regions.
Stars shine with their own light
Constellation: pattern (earlier) / region of sky (now) — 88 in all
Orion, Canis Major (Sirius), Taurus, Ursa Major, Ursa Minor

The Pole Star (Dhruva tārā), in the Little Dipper, appears nearly stationary in the North, so it shows the North direction in the Northern hemisphere; it is found by following the two end stars of the Big Dipper's cup.
Pole Star = Dhruva tārā, in the Little Dipper
Nearly stationary in the North → shows North
Big Dipper's two end stars × 5 gaps → Pole Star
Stars are best seen from dark, open places on clear, moonless nights; light pollution, smoke, dust, clouds and buildings hide them. Apps, preparation and instruments help us find what we want to see.
Dark, open, clear, moonless → more stars
Apps tell when and where to look
Wait ~30 minutes; always go with adults
Orion's belt → Sirius
The Sun is a star — the closest one — a hot ball of gases giving heat and light. It looks big and hides other stars by day only because it is so much closer than the other stars.
Sun = nearest star
~100 × Earth's diameter; ~150 million km = 1 au
Closer → looks bigger and brighter; hides stars by day

A planet is a large, nearly spherical object that revolves around the Sun. There are eight: four small rocky inner planets and four giant outer planets of gas and ice; stars twinkle a lot while planets hardly twinkle.
Planet: large, nearly spherical, revolves around the Sun
Order: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars | Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune
Inner: small, rocky · Outer: giant, gas and ice, rings
Stars twinkle a lot; planets hardly twinkle

Objects that move around planets are satellites; moons are natural satellites. Earth's Moon goes around Earth in about 27 days, is a quarter of Earth's diameter, has hardly any atmosphere and is covered with craters.
Satellite: moves around a planet; moons are natural satellites
Moon: 27 days, ¼ Earth's diameter, 3,84,000 km, hardly any atmosphere
Craters stay because there is no air, water or life
Asteroids are small, rocky, irregular objects, many revolving between Mars and Jupiter. Comets are icy-rocky visitors from far away whose frozen material evaporates into a long tail near the Sun.
Asteroids: small, rocky, irregular; belt between Mars and Jupiter
Comets: dust, gas, rock, ice; tail near the Sun
Halley's Comet: every 76 years, last 1986

notes.h: Our Solar System — All Members Together
items: The Sun, eight planets, their moons and smaller objects such as asteroids and comets form the Solar System. Only the Sun makes light and energy; all others shine by reflecting sunlight.
The Sun is the largest and heaviest object of the Solar System and produces almost all its energy
All other objects shine due to the sunlight they reflect

notes.h: The Milky Way Galaxy and the Universe
items: Our Solar System is part of the Milky Way Galaxy — millions to billions of stars, seen as a faint band of light on dark nights. The Universe has many galaxies; scientists search exoplanets for life but have found no evidence yet.

items.text: There are many galaxies in outer space beyond the Milky Way; scientists study them to understand stars, galaxies and the Universe

items: No evidence of life elsewhere has been found yet — the search continues
Wrong: The lines of a constellation can be seen in the sky. Right: The lines are imaginary — drawn only to identify the pattern
Wrong: The Pole Star is the brightest star in the sky. Right: It is not very bright; Sirius is the brightest star of the night sky
Wrong: Cities have fewer stars above them. Right: The stars are there; light pollution, smoke and dust hide them
Wrong: The Sun is not a star — stars are tiny dots. Right: The Sun is a star; it looks big only because it is the closest
Wrong: Venus is a star because it is called the Morning Star. Right: Venus is a planet; the name only says when it is seen
Wrong: Only Earth has a moon. Right: Mars has two moons and the giant planets have many

sol_items: Are star patterns the same for everyone? Why not?: No. People imagine different shapes and stories.
Do we find patterns just for fun?: They also help us to find stars, direction and time of the year.
If the Sun is a star, why does it look so big?: It is very close to us; other stars are very far away so they look like dots.
Why do stars fade at dawn and appear at dusk?: Stars are always in the sky but sunlight is too bright for us to see them by day.
How to find north using the Pole Star: Find the Big Dipper and follow its pointer stars to the Pole Star, which shows north.
How can we tell planets from stars?: Stars twinkle; planets shine steadily and change places among the stars.

A group of stars forming a pattern
Why do stars twinkle but planets do not?
Stars are very far and look like points of light
How do we find the Pole Star?
Follow the pointer stars of the Big Dipper
What does the Pole Star show?
The north direction
Why are stars not seen in the day?
Sunlight is too bright
What is the Sun?
The nearest star, a hot ball of gases
